title: test-0120-GEN-MANGALYAAN
passage: Rohan and his sister Meera sat on their terrace in Bengaluru, looking at the night sky. Meera asked, 'Why do we need Aditya-L1 to study the Sun from space when we have telescopes on Earth?' Rohan explained that Earth’s atmosphere blocks harmful UV and X-ray radiation, so we must go to space to observe them. He added that Aditya-L1 is not landing on the Sun, which would be impossible due to the intense heat, but is instead positioned at the L1 Lagrange point to get an uninterrupted view. Meera then recalled Mangalyaan, India’s Mars Orbiter Mission. She wondered if it was launched by the massive GSLV Mk III. Rohan corrected her, noting that the cost-effective PSLV rocket launched Mangalyaan, making it a budget-friendly success. He explained that the spacecraft didn't just float; it used precise engine burns to adjust its speed and enter Mars' orbit. 'It wasn't just for show,' Rohan said, 'it carried scientific instruments to study the Martian atmosphere and surface, proving India’s capability for deep-space exploration.' Meera realized that space missions are about complex engineering, not just luck or simple travel. They watched the stars, imagining the spacecraft silently working millions of kilometers away, held in place by the delicate balance of gravity.
summary: Rohan and his sister Meera sat on their terrace in Bengaluru, looking at the night sky. Rohan explained that the Earth’s atmosphere blocks harmful UV and X-ray radiation, so we should go to space to observe them.
